extracted.intended_audience: law students and patent practitioners (attorneys, judges) studying or applying early U.S. patent statutes
extracted.subtask_description: Statutory requirements and procedural rules from early U.S. patent acts (1790–1794) covering patentability, specification and model requirements, fees, enforcement remedies, challenges, interference resolution, assignments, and related procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability — novelty and usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention or discovery must be 'not before known or used' and be a 'useful art, machine, manufacture, engine, or device, or any improvement therein not before known or used.' (Acts repeatedly require inventions to be 'new and useful' and not known or used either in this or any foreign country.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must allege the invention is new and useful; later statutes require oath/affirmation that, to the best of applicant's knowledge or belief, the invention 'hath not been known or used either in this or any foreign country.' A patent later shown to have been known or used before application is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and models — full, clear, exact disclosure (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grantee must deliver 'a specification in writing, containing a description, accompanied with explanations and models (if the nature of the invention will admit of a model) ... so particular, and said models so exact, as not only to distinguish the invention ... from other things before known and used, but also to enable a workman or other person skilled in the art ... to make, construct, or use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must be 'so full, clear, and exact' as to enable persons skilled in the art. For machines, explain the principle and 'the several modes' of application; include drawings and written references when drawings admit; for compositions, provide specimens sufficient for experiment. Specifications are to be filed and certified copies are 'competent evidence' in courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's oath/affirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every inventor, before presenting his invention, 'shall swear or affirm, that he does verily believe, that he is the true inventor or discoverer' and (in later provisions) that the invention 'hath not ... been known or used either in this or any foreign country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath/affirmation may be made before any person authorized to administer oaths; false statements may render the patent void and enable repeal proceedings. Alien applicants receiving privileges must likewise make the required oath/affirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term (duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted 'for any term not exceeding fourteen years' (the Acts provide a term of up to fourteen years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early U.S. patent grants under these acts were limited to a maximum fourteen-year term; statutes and practice should be read to determine precise term and any continuity or renewal provisions in specific enactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification formalities — signatures, witnesses, drawings, and filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description is to be 'signed by himself and attested by two witnesses' and filed in the office of the Secretary (or Attorney General), with drawings where nature of the case admits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models are required when deemed necessary; drawings and written references must accompany machine specifications; compositions require specimens sufficient for experiment. Certified copies of filed specifications serve as court evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and office fees (pre-grant and copying fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees specified include: for receiving and filing petition fifty cents; for filing specifications per 100 words ten cents; for making out patent two dollars; affixing great seal one dollar; indorsing day of delivery twenty cents. Later provisions require a payment (e.g., thirty dollars) to the treasury on presenting petition and copying fees (20 cents per 100 words; $2 per drawing copy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must pay the prescribed fees before patent issuance; copying fees for records are charged to parties obtaining copies. Fee schedules differ across the acts and must be followed precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement remedies — injunctions, damages, forfeiture, treble penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit courts may grant injunctions 'according to the course and principles of courts of equity' to prevent violation; infringers shall 'forfeit and pay ... such damages as shall be assessed by a jury' and may forfeit the thing(s) so devised, made, constructed, used, employed, or vended. In one Act the penalty is at least 'equal to three times the price' for which the patentee usually sold or licensed the use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief includes equitable injunctions and legal damages; statutes provide for recovery of infringing items and, in some provisions, enhanced (treble) damages. Remedies depend on compliance with procedural rules and venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction of federal courts and appellate practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases 'granting or confirming to inventors exclusive right' shall be originally cognizable 'as well in equity as at law' by the circuit courts of the United States (and district courts having similar powers). That jurisdiction 'embraces all cases, both at law and in equity, arising under the patent laws' and is treated as exclusive; appeals lie to the Supreme Court, and when a case is sent up the whole case is to go up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit courts have original jurisdiction over patent matters; state courts generally cannot entertain patent infringement suits. Appeals to the Supreme Court under statutory discretion should bring up the whole case rather than isolated points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary rule in actions — patents/specifications prima facie; defendant's defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: In actions for penalties, 'the said patents or specifications shall be prima facie evidence, that the said patentee ... was the first and true inventor ... and that the same is truly specified; but ... the defendant may plead the general issue, and give this act, and any special matter ... in evidence' with prior written notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and filed specifications create a presumption of validity and priority, but defendants may rebut by pleading general issue and adducing special matter (e.g., prior use, concealment, overclaiming). Statutes require notice (30 days) for special matter to be offered at trial; proven concealment or material overstatement intended to mislead can lead to verdict for defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging patents obtained surreptitiously or by false suggestion — repeal procedure and time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon oath or affirmation that a patent 'was obtained surreptitiously by, or upon false suggestion,' the judge of the district court may, within prescribed time limits (one year under one act; three years under another), grant a rule to show cause why process should not issue to repeal such patent; if sufficient cause not shown, judgment for repeal is entered and costs may be awarded against the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes set temporal windows for collaterally attacking issuance on grounds of fraud or surreptitious procurement. Courts will require sufficient showing before ordering repeal; if the challenger loses, they may be liable for defendant's costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering applications — arbitration procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of interfering applications, they 'shall be submitted to the arbitration of three persons, one of whom shall be chosen by each of the applicants, and the third person shall be appointed by the Secretary of State; the decision or award of such arbitrators ... shall be final as far as respects the granting of the patent.' If an applicant refuses to choose an arbitrator, the patent issues to the opposite party; when more than two applicants exist the Secretary may appoint arbitrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference resolution is by appointed arbitrators whose written award controls grant. Failure to participate risks losing the patent; Secretary has authority to appoint arbitrators when applicants do not agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments and recording — assignee steps into inventor's place
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be lawful for any inventor to assign their title and interest; 'the assignee having recorded the said assignment in the office of the Secretary of State, shall thereafter stand in the place of the original inventor, both as to right and responsibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments should be recorded in the patent office records to effectuate standing; recording changes rights and responsibilities to the assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-granted rights and federal patent entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any State before adoption of the present government 'shall have granted an exclusive right to any invention,' the claimant cannot obtain an exclusive right under this act except on relinquishing his right under such particular State; relinquishment and obtaining under the act is sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior state-granted exclusivities must be relinquished to secure federal patent rights under the act; the statute requires clear relinquishment before federal grant will be recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements and trivial alterations — scope of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who discovers an improvement on the principle of a machine or process may obtain a patent for such improvement, but 'simply changing the form or the proportions of any machine, or composition of matter, in any degree, shall not be deemed a discovery.' Also, provisions recognize interplay between original inventors and improvement patentees regarding rights to make or vend original or improved forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor form or proportion changes are not patentable discoveries. The statute contemplates limits and potential exclusivity conflicts between original inventors and subsequent improvers; rights to practice original vs. improved forms depend on the specific grants and any necessary licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of specifications and permission to make similar models
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon application to the Secretary of State for a copy of any specification and permission to have similar model(s) made, 'it shall be the duty of the Secretary to give such copy, and to permit the person so applying ... to take, or make, or cause the same to be taken or made, at the expense of such applicant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties may obtain certified copies of specifications and, with permission and at their expense, make similar models; the office must provide copies and access under the stated conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional provisions for prior pending applications or suits after repeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons whose applications or suits were pending under former law may, on complying with the conditions of the new act and paying required fees, pursue their claims; suits set aside or abated by repeal may be restored within one year of the later act, with parties brought into court as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes provide mechanisms to preserve and restore pending claims and proceedings affected by repeal of prior patent acts. Parties must follow reinstitution procedures (e.g., bringing parties into court by summons) and comply with new-act conditions and fees.
